_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
tosafot:a1.1: How do I realize “of which they may not bring an offering”? With blemished animals, that they can be redeemed: And one cannot say, interpret it the other way round, for the verse “of which they may not bring” implies that it is disqualified only from being offered, but is permitted for ordinary use.
rashi:a3.1: And the Merciful One states: perform standing and valuation for it: as it is written after it, “then he shall set … and shall value.” And this is certainly [an animal] consecrated for the altar, since we require a permanent blemish; for if it were [consecrated for] Temple maintenance, unblemished animals too are redeemed, for what does it matter to them whether it is unblemished or blemished? Evidently, according to the Rabbis, animals consecrated for the altar too were included in standing and valuation, since this baraita is the Rabbis’: it is an unattributed Sifra, and an unattributed Sifra is Rabbi Yehuda (Bekhorot 61a), the disputant of Rabbi Shimon; and this is in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan. And from here we learn [the Rabbis’ view on] animals consecrated for the altar, and from the mishna we learn [their view on] those consecrated for Temple maintenance: since Rabbi Shimon says that those consecrated for Temple maintenance are redeemed, it follows that we have heard the Rabbis say they are buried.
tosafot:a3.1: And the Merciful One states: perform standing and valuation for it: since in this verse, “of which they may not bring,” it is written “then he shall set … and shall value,” and an unattributed Sifra is Rabbi Yehuda. Evidently the Rabbis in general hold that standing applies to animals consecrated for the altar. And [that it applies to] animals consecrated for Temple maintenance we know from the mishna, since Rabbi Shimon says they are redeemed, which implies that according to the Rabbis they are not redeemed. Alternatively, we know [it for] animals consecrated for Temple maintenance from what is written, “And the priest shall value it, whether it be good or bad”: which is an item in which there is no distinction between good and bad? You must say, this is [an item] consecrated for Temple maintenance. [The note ends with the letters ר״ש.]
rashi:a4.1: Whether it be good or bad: implies good and bad alike, that the two are equal, the unblemished and the blemished.
rashi:a5.1: “It” serves to exclude animals consecrated for the altar: and this “then he shall set … and shall value” does not refer back to the first part of the verse, which speaks of animals consecrated for the altar.
gershom:a1.1: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said that according to the Rabbis both this and that were included in standing and valuation [the daf names Reish Lakish here, and the reasoning that follows is his]? As it is written: “And if it be any non-kosher animal” etc. Which is an item that is not divided between good and bad, that is, whose sanctity is the same whether it is unblemished or blemished? That is [an item] consecrated for Temple maintenance, which is only for its value. And it is written “it”: “and the priest shall value it,” to exclude animals consecrated for the altar. And Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that “it,” according to the Rabbis, serves to exclude an animal blemished from the outset, which is not included in standing and valuation. Another version: [the Gemara] teaches, What is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon, who said that animals consecrated for the altar were [included] and animals consecrated for Temple maintenance were not, as we said above; and both this one and that one agree, etc.
rashi:a6.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan: certainly holds that this “whether it be good or bad” refers to animals consecrated for Temple maintenance. But “then he shall set … and shall value” refers both to the first part of the verse, which we established as speaking of animals consecrated for the altar, and to the latter part, which speaks of Temple maintenance; and “it” serves to exclude an animal blemished from the outset among animals consecrated for the altar. And according to Reish Lakish there is no need to exclude an animal blemished from the outset, since he says that according to the Rabbis animals consecrated for the altar were not [included], even where their consecration preceded their blemish, and all the more so this one.
rashi:a7.1: And even undomesticated animals and birds: such as geese and chickens, which have no connection to the altar at all.
tosafot:a7.1: Even an undomesticated animal and even a bird: for example, where one associates chickens [with a consecration] for Temple maintenance. And that which we say in Menaḥot (100b), “Birds have no redemption,” applies where they were consecrated with inherent sanctity for the altar.
rashi:a9.1: It should have said “between good and bad”: that would imply that there is a distinction between good and bad; but “whether good or bad” implies good and bad alike, the two being equal.
gershom:a2.1: Which is an item that is divided between good and bad, between unblemished and blemished? These are animals consecrated for the altar, for an unblemished one is offered and a blemished one is not. And it is written “it”: “and the priest shall value it,” to exclude animals consecrated for Temple maintenance. If so, according to Rabbi Shimon, [instead of] “whether good or bad” it should have written “between good and bad.” If it speaks of animals consecrated for the altar, it is difficult for Rabbi Shimon.
rashi:a10.1: If they died unblemished, they shall be buried: even those that are not included in standing and valuation, where they died unblemished, the Rabbis made a stringency that they be buried, since they were fit for sacrifice.
rashi:a10.2: With regard to animals consecrated for the altar: it now enters our mind [that blemished ones are redeemed] because they were not included in standing and valuation.
rashi:a10.3: But with regard to animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, etc.: since they were [included] in standing and valuation.
tosafot:a10.1: Unblemished ones shall be buried; blemished ones can be redeemed: it now enters our mind [that this is] because animals consecrated for the altar were not included in standing and valuation; and unblemished ones are buried because they have no blemish, and one is not permitted to redeem without a blemish.
gershom:a3.1: They raised an objection: animals consecrated for the altar, unblemished ones are buried and blemished ones are redeemed; animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, both unblemished and blemished ones are buried. And this baraita is precise in accordance with Reish Lakish according to the Rabbis [the printed text reads “according to Rabbi Shimon,” corrected to “the Rabbis”], who said that animals consecrated for Temple maintenance were [included] and animals consecrated for the altar were not.
rashi:a11.1: Rabbi Shimon says, etc.: unblemished ones shall be buried: as a stringency.
rashi:a11.2: And blemished ones can be redeemed: further on the Gemara asks: how can Rabbi Shimon say that animals consecrated for the altar [are redeemed], when both Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish say that according to Rabbi Shimon animals consecrated for the altar were included in standing and valuation?
tosafot:a11.1: Rabbi Shimon says: unblemished ones shall be buried: for even though animals consecrated for Temple maintenance were not [included], [they are buried], as the reason is explained below: because they are fit for sacrifice.
rashi:a11.3: A conclusive refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan from the first clause: which teaches that according to the Rabbis, animals consecrated for the altar are redeemed.
gershom:a4.1: Rabbi Shimon says: Both animals consecrated, etc. Is it not speaking of one that was unblemished [when consecrated], when it teaches that blemished ones are redeemed? Is it not teaching [a case] where their consecration preceded their blemish? And it is difficult for Rabbi Yoḥanan from the first clause of the baraita, which teaches that blemished ones are redeemed; for Rabbi Yoḥanan said that according to the Rabbis both animals consecrated for the altar and those consecrated for Temple maintenance were included in standing and valuation, so that they are buried, and [the baraita] speaks of where their consecration preceded their blemish, yet this baraita teaches that they are redeemed. And it is a conclusive refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan from the first clause.
rashi:a12.1: With an animal blemished from the outset: that is why they are redeemed, while those consecrated for Temple maintenance are buried, for there no distinction is made between an animal blemished from the outset and one whose consecration preceded its blemish.
tosafot:a12.1: What are we dealing with here? With an animal blemished from the outset: and even so, animals consecrated for Temple maintenance are buried, since they were [included] in every case; for it is not relevant to distinguish between one that was unblemished at the outset and one blemished from the outset, since they stand only for their value.
gershom:a5.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you: What are we dealing with here in the first clause, that they are redeemed? With animals blemished from the outset, which according to everyone were not included in standing and valuation.
rashi:a13.1: So too it is reasonable, for if [it speaks] where their consecration preceded their blemish: and the Rabbis’ reason is as Reish Lakish says, that animals consecrated for the altar were not included in standing and valuation, then Rabbi Shimon should disagree with it and say that animals consecrated for the altar are buried, since according to Rabbi Shimon animals consecrated for the altar were [included] in standing and valuation. Rather, since he does not disagree, conclude from it that it refers to an animal blemished from the outset; and that is why animals consecrated for the altar are redeemed, and animals consecrated for Temple maintenance are also redeemed, since according to Rabbi Shimon animals consecrated for Temple maintenance were not [included].
gershom:a6.1: So too it is reasonable that it is with an animal blemished from the outset; for if it says they are redeemed where their consecration preceded their blemish…
gershom:a7.1: Rabbi Shimon should disagree with the first clause and say that they are buried, since we said that both this one and that one agree that according to Rabbi Shimon animals consecrated for the altar were included in standing and valuation.
rashi:a14.1: Let us say it is a conclusive refutation of Reish Lakish: since from the baraita itself we learn that it refers to an animal blemished from the outset; and now one can say: the reason is that it was blemished from the outset, but where its consecration preceded its blemish, according to the Rabbis too they are buried.
gershom:a8.1: Another version: the latter clause is difficult for Rabbi Shimon of the mishna, since in the latter clause of this baraita it says: “Rabbi Shimon says: Both animals consecrated for the altar and animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, unblemished ones are buried and blemished ones are redeemed”; and Rabbi Shimon contradicts Rabbi Shimon, since Rabbi Shimon said above that animals consecrated for the altar were [included]. Rather, must one not conclude from it that in the latter clause too, where Rabbi Shimon says blemished ones are redeemed, he is speaking of an animal blemished from the outset, which was not included in standing and valuation? And now he infers from the baraita: but where their consecration preceded their blemish, what [is the law]? It requires standing and valuation. Let us say it is a conclusive refutation of Reish Lakish, since he said above that according to the Rabbis animals consecrated for the altar were not [included].
rashi:a15.1: Where their consecration preceded their blemish: and the Rabbis’ reason is that animals consecrated for the altar were not [included].
gershom:a9.1: Reish Lakish establishes it above, according to the Rabbis, where their consecration preceded their blemish; and even so, according to the Rabbis, animals consecrated for the altar were not [included], and here too they were not, and so they are redeemed.
rashi:a15.2: Rabbi Shimon should disagree with it: regarding animals consecrated for the altar, and say that they are buried. So why does it teach that according to Rabbi Shimon both animals consecrated for the altar and those consecrated for Temple maintenance are redeemed?
gershom:a10.1: If so, our difficulty returns: Rabbi Shimon should disagree in the first clause, since he said that animals consecrated for the altar were [included]. And further, the latter clause, Rabbi Shimon’s, is difficult against the first clause.
rashi:a16.1: And Reish Lakish answers: he reverses it, and raises the objection like this from another collection: for he found another baraita that reverses it, and he raises the objection to Rabbi Yoḥanan from it in this way. For Reish Lakish does not bring this objection against Rabbi Yoḥanan as we read [the baraita] here, since it teaches explicitly according to Rabbi Shimon that animals consecrated for the altar are redeemed.
tosafot:a16.1: Reish Lakish removes it and teaches [it] from another collection: and the one above is erroneous. Rather [the baraita reads]: “Whether unblemished or blemished, they shall be buried,” and it speaks of animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, in accordance with the Rabbis, who say that they were [included, etc.]. “Rabbi Shimon says: [Unblemished ones] shall be buried,” as is said below, because they are fit for sacrifice, and one treats them stringently with the sanctity of the altar. “In what case is this statement said? With regard to animals consecrated for Temple maintenance”: this returns to the first tanna, and that is why he said “buried”; “but animals consecrated for the altar, etc.” “Rabbi Shimon says: Unblemished ones shall be buried, but blemished ones can be redeemed,” since they were not included in standing. “A conclusive refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan”; “Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you, etc.”; “A conclusive refutation of Reish Lakish”; “Indeed, Rabbi Shimon disagrees.” And Rashi pointed out that for the first baraita too we could say so; so what advantage does this latter one have? One can say that they are not alike, for of the first one this cannot be said. If the first tanna’s blemished animals were ones that became blemished after their consecration, and [the ruling] concerns animals consecrated for the altar, it is reasonable to say that Rabbi Shimon, who says in his own statement “both animals consecrated for the altar [and those for Temple maintenance] are redeemed,” is speaking of the first tanna’s blemished animals, which became blemished after they were consecrated. But in this latter baraita, Rabbi Shimon does not speak of animals consecrated for the altar at all in his statement; it is in the separate statement of the Rabbis, who say “but with regard to animals consecrated for the altar, blemished ones are redeemed,” that it fits well [to speak of] where their consecration preceded [their blemish], and Rabbi Shimon disagrees with them. And the tanna taught his statement this way because in it he did not mention animals consecrated for the altar at all, and did not reveal at all what he says about them.
gershom:a11.1: Reish Lakish could say to you: teach in the latter clause of this baraita, regarding animals consecrated for the altar, that Rabbi Shimon says: whether unblemished or blemished, they are buried; and there is no difficulty.
rashi:a16.2: Rather, he reverses it, and raises the objection to it as we found in another collection: “whether unblemished,” etc.: And although, when you examine it closely, there is no difference between this version and the version above, except that [the first one] teaches explicitly that according to Rabbi Shimon animals consecrated for the altar are redeemed.
gershom:a12.1: Another version: Reish Lakish reverses this baraita, and raises the objection like this from a collection, another baraita. And he raises the objection like this: They raised an objection: “If they died, whether unblemished or blemished, they shall be buried. Rabbi Shimon says: Unblemished ones are buried, blemished ones are redeemed.”
gershom:a13.1: In what case is this statement said: he returns to the first tanna. In what case is this statement said, that whether unblemished or blemished they are buried? With regard to animals consecrated for Temple maintenance; but with regard to animals consecrated for the altar, [blemished ones are redeemed]. And this is precise in accordance with Reish Lakish according to the Rabbis.
rashi:a17.1: In what case is this statement said: that the first tanna says blemished ones are buried? With regard to animals consecrated for Temple maintenance; but animals consecrated for the altar are redeemed, since they were not [included] in standing and valuation. And Rabbi Shimon comes to disagree about animals consecrated for Temple maintenance: you said they are buried; according to me they are redeemed.
rashi:a17.2: A conclusive refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan from this latter clause: which teaches, according to the first tanna: but animals consecrated for the altar are redeemed.
gershom:a14.1: Is it not where their consecration preceded their blemish that it speaks? And it is a conclusive refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan from this latter clause, “In what case.”
rashi:a18.1: With an animal blemished from the outset: and [an animal consecrated for] Temple maintenance is buried, since there we make no distinction between one that was unblemished at the outset and one blemished from the outset.
gershom:a15.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you: What are we dealing with here, that blemished ones are redeemed? With animals blemished from the outset.
rashi:a18.2: Rabbi Shimon should disagree with it: and say two things: animals consecrated for Temple maintenance are redeemed, and animals consecrated for the altar are buried. Rather, since he disagrees only about animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, where they say buried and he says redeemed, while about animals consecrated for the altar he is silent regarding what the Rabbis say, that they are redeemed, conclude from it that it speaks of an animal blemished from the outset.
gershom:a16.1: So too it is reasonable: for if you do not say so, Rabbi Shimon should disagree regarding animals consecrated for the altar, that blemished ones are buried, since he holds that animals consecrated for the altar were [included].
gershom:a17.1: Rather, conclude from it: it speaks of animals blemished from the outset.
rashi:a19.1: Indeed, he disagrees: and the tanna taught you their dispute about Temple maintenance, and the same is true that he disagrees with them also about animals consecrated for the altar, [saying] that they are buried.
gershom:a18.1: But where their consecration preceded their blemish, what [is the law]? It requires standing and valuation. Let us say it is, etc., as we said above. If so, Rabbi Shimon should disagree in the latter clause of the baraita, which teaches: but with regard to animals consecrated for the altar, blemished ones are redeemed; and Rabbi Shimon should say that they are buried, as he holds. Reish Lakish could say to you: teach in the latter clause, regarding animals consecrated for the altar, [whether unblemished or blemished, they are buried]. Since they are fit for the altar by means of redemption, they made a stringency for them, that they be buried, since they do not leave the custody of the altar.
rashi:a20.1: According to Reish Lakish, who says that according to the Rabbis, etc.: that which is taught in this baraita, that animals consecrated for the altar are redeemed, he establishes even where their consecration preceded their blemish; conclude from it, etc. Granted, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who establishes it as referring to an animal blemished from the outset, it does not matter to us if it is redeemed for dogs, since sanctity never took effect on its body. But according to Reish Lakish there is a question.
gershom:b1.1: Conclude from it that one may redeem sacrificial animals to feed them to dogs: since once they have died and he redeems them, they are fit only for dogs.
rashi:b2.1: What are we dealing with here: that which is taught, “if they died,” does not mean they actually died, but that one transgressed and slaughtered them before redemption; about these it says they are redeemed and eaten.
gershom:b2.1: Rather, what are we dealing with here? Where one transgressed and slaughtered them before redemption, so that now, when he redeems them, they are fit to be eaten.
tosafot:b3.1: In brief: As it is taught: all sacrificial animals that developed a blemish and one slaughtered them, Rabbi Meir says: they shall be buried: this speaks of animals consecrated for the altar; Rabbi Meir holds they were included in standing, like Rabbi Shimon (and according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, like the Rabbis too), and the Rabbis say they are redeemed because they were not included. For Reish Lakish this works well: these are the Rabbis of the mishna. But for Rabbi Yoḥanan, who says that according to both the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon altar animals were included, who are the Rabbis here? One cannot say the case is a blemish that preceded consecration and they disagree as the tanna of the school of Levi does, for at the end of chapter HaNehene Min HaHekdesh (Me’ila 19b) the reading is explicit: altar animals that were unblemished and became blemished, and one slaughtered them: Rabbi Meir says buried, the Rabbis say redeemed. The books add: Rabbi Meir is like Rabbi Shimon, the Rabbis here are like the Rabbis there; let it be a refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan; Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that the Rabbis here are one group and the Rabbis there another. The baraita here could instead be deflected as speaking of Temple maintenance, with “the Rabbis” being Rabbi Shimon; but in Me’ila it is taught of unblemished altar animals: Rabbi says buried, the Rabbis say redeemed, and there the only answer is that the two groups of Rabbis differ. Why would Rabbi Yoḥanan accept three disputes rather than say the Rabbis here are like the Rabbis there, that altar animals were not included? Because the mishna is difficult: since Rabbi Shimon had to specify that animals consecrated for Temple maintenance that died are redeemed, the first tanna must have spoken of them, as the books explain the whole passage. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b3.1: Rabbi Meir says: they shall be buried: like Rabbi Shimon, who says that animals consecrated for the altar were [included] in standing and valuation.
rashi:b3.2: They can be redeemed: since they were not [included] in standing and valuation.
gershom:b3.1: As it is taught, etc. And the Rabbis say: they can be redeemed. Since Rabbi Meir [holds] like Rabbi Shimon, who says that animals consecrated for the altar were [included], they are buried.
gershom:b4.1: The Rabbis here, who say they are redeemed, are like the Rabbis there above, according to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who said that animals consecrated for the altar were not [included], and so they are redeemed.
rashi:b4.1: Because they are fit for sacrifice: they made a stringency for them, for unblemished animals [that are fit] for the altar.
tosafot:b4.1: Because they are fit for sacrifice: And it is difficult: if so, what does it say in the first chapter of Shevuot (11b) about a red heifer that was slaughtered, that it is redeemed? [The Gemara there] asks: but standing [and valuation] is required, etc.; and it establishes it in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who says that animals consecrated for Temple maintenance were not [included]. But what of it? It is unblemished, and it should have said that it is buried! One can say that there is a distinction in the matter. Certainly, when one consecrated unblemished animals for Temple maintenance, he transgressed the prohibition against consecrating them [for Temple maintenance] and deviated with them, consecrating them not in accordance with their mitzva, since the mitzva for unblemished animals is the altar; it is proper to bury them when they died. But a red heifer, with which he did not deviate from its mitzva, is redeemed. (Why did he take it? Alternatively, one can say: certainly with unblemished animals for Temple maintenance, which stand to go to the altar, we must be stringent, as you said, “[fit for] the altar.”)
rashi:b6.1: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who establishes it as referring to an animal blemished from the outset: and says that is why Rabbi Shimon does not disagree with it; evidently, according to everyone, an animal blemished from the outset does not require standing and valuation. But we learned, etc. Granted, according to Reish Lakish there is no difficulty, since he establishes it as an unblemished animal that became blemished after consecration, and one can say that an animal blemished from the outset is like a consecration for Temple maintenance: although he consecrated it for the altar, it is nevertheless like Temple maintenance, since it is consecrated only for its value, and it is [included] in standing and valuation according to the Rabbis. But according to Rabbi Yoḥanan it is difficult.
rashi:b7.1: And in the gifts: the foreleg, the jaw and the maw.
rashi:b7.2: To be shorn and to be utilized for labor: after their redemption.
rashi:b8.1: Their offspring and their milk are permitted: even if [the offspring] was conceived before their redemption and born after their redemption.
rashi:b9.1: And Rav said: about it, in the second chapter of Bekhorot: that which we learned, “they may be redeemed,” is the statement of Rabbi Shimon, who says that animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, if they died, are redeemed; and he considers this animal blemished from the outset like animals consecrated for Temple maintenance. But the Rabbis, etc.
gershom:b5.1: [An editorial note says this is Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading as given in the Shitah Mekubetzet.] Let us say it is a conclusive refutation, etc. This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon, who says that animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, if they died, are redeemed, since they were not included in standing and valuation. And these consecrated animals whose blemish preceded their consecration, even though they are consecrated for the altar, since a full consecration for the altar did not take effect on them, their law is therefore like that of animals consecrated for Temple maintenance: if they died they are redeemed, since they were not included in standing and valuation.
gershom:b6.1: But the Sages say: all were included [in standing and valuation], even animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, even one blemished from the outset. And this is difficult for Rabbi Yoḥanan, who says that “it,” according to the Rabbis, serves to exclude one blemished from the outset, which was not [included]; for it now enters our mind that these Sages are the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon.
gershom:b7.1: He said to him: No. Who are the Sages? The tanna of the school of Levi. But the Rabbis in the dispute with Rabbi Shimon hold, with regard to animals blemished from the outset, like Rabbi Shimon.
rashi:b11.1: And his disputants: since you have established that the Rabbis who disagree with him also [hold] that an animal blemished from the outset was not included in standing and valuation. [And] the reason Rav did not say “this is the statement of Rabbi Shimon and his disputants” is that he holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who said that according to the Rabbis animals consecrated for the altar were not included in standing and valuation. Therefore that [mishna] in Bekhorot cannot be established entirely according to the Rabbis: its first clause, which speaks of an animal blemished from the outset and teaches “they may be redeemed,” can be established even according to the Rabbis; but the latter clause teaches, “But sacrificial animals whose consecration preceded their blemish, if they died, they shall be buried,” which does not accord with the Rabbis. Therefore it cannot be established according to the Rabbis here.
gershom:b8.1: If so, “this is the statement of Rabbi Shimon” — Rav should have said “and his disputants.” Rava said to him [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text names Rava as the one who answers]: Rav holds like Reish Lakish, who says that according to the Rabbis animals consecrated for the altar were not [included], and the latter clause cannot be established according to the Rabbis, since it teaches: where their consecration preceded their blemish, if they died, they shall be buried. If it were the Rabbis, since they say that animals consecrated for the altar were not [included], why would they be buried? Therefore he cannot say “this is the statement of Rabbi Shimon and his disputants.” But according to Rabbi Shimon the latter clause too can be established, since both Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish agree that according to Rabbi Shimon animals consecrated for the altar were [included]; therefore, when their consecration preceded their blemish, they are buried. But with an animal blemished from the outset, that is, where its blemish preceded its consecration, Rabbi Shimon concedes that it was not included, and it is redeemed.
rashi:b14.1: And if you wish, say that Rav holds like Rabbi Yoḥanan: that both animals consecrated for the altar and those consecrated for Temple maintenance require standing and valuation, except for an animal blemished from the outset; and both the first and the latter clauses of that [mishna] can be established also according to the Rabbis, as well as according to Rabbi Shimon, and he teaches: “This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon and his disputants.”
gershom:b9.1: And if you wish, say: you may even say that Rav holds like Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said that according to the Rabbis both this and that were [included], and they agree with regard to an animal blemished from the outset that it was not.
gershom:b10.1: And as for what was difficult for you: if so, the first and latter clauses can be established also according to the Rabbis, so let him say “this is the statement of Rabbi Shimon and his disputants”; teach it so, and there is no difficulty.
rashi:b15.1: Mishna: they shall be buried: the miscarried fetuses.
rashi:b15.2: A placenta shall be buried: since there is no placenta without a fetus. And all of these are buried because they are forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b11.1: Mishna: These are the items that are buried: for all of these are forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b13.1: [This note concerns the Gemara on 34a, which contrasts this mishna with a mishna in Orla.] There is no difficulty: that which is taught, “and from a firstborn donkey, in a sack, it shall be burned,” is where he wove the hair into a sack; for if you say it is buried, sometimes a person may find it and use it; therefore it is burned. That is with [woven] hair; but the hair of a firstborn donkey that is not woven is buried, for even if it comes into a person’s hands afterward, he will leave it, as it is not fit for anything. And “in a dispute”: this “in a dispute” is like “as tanna’im,” except that because Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, was an Amora, he used this expression “in a dispute.”
rashi:b16.1: Non-sacred animals that were slaughtered in the courtyard shall be burned: because sacrificial animals that incurred a disqualification would be confused with them. For if he said they are buried, since it is not evident whether they were non-sacred or sacrificial, people would come to say that sacrificial animals that incurred a disqualification of impurity or of notar are also buried. And we hold, in the second chapter of Pesaḥim (24a), that “In the holy place… it shall be burned with fire” [Leviticus 6:23] teaches about all the disqualified [items] among consecrated items, that they are to be burned.
rashi:b16.2: And likewise an undomesticated animal that was slaughtered in the courtyard: even if it is non-sacred, where there is no [reason] to decree lest people bury disqualified sacrificial animals, since everyone knows that there are no undomesticated animals among consecrated animals and they will not come to confuse them; even so it is burned.
gershom:b12.1: Rabbi Shimon says: non-sacred animals that were slaughtered in the courtyard shall be burned. What is the reason they are burned? Because their law is like that of sacrificial animals that were slaughtered outside their place: just as those are burned because their manner was changed, so too non-sacred animals whose manner was changed are burned. And from where do we derive that sacrificial animals slaughtered outside their place [are burned]? As it is written: “And any sin offering whose blood is brought,” etc. [Leviticus 6:23]; this teaches that anything whose place was changed is burned. [The rest of the note concerns the Gemara on 34a.] There is no difficulty: this is with an impure nazirite, that is with a pure nazirite. That which is taught, “from the hair of a nazirite, in a sack, it shall be burned,” is with the hair of an impure nazirite [a correction reads: pure], since his law is to send it under the pot and burn it; therefore it is burned. And that which is taught, “it shall be buried,” is with the hair of a pure nazirite [a correction reads: impure].
rashi:b17.1: Leavened bread on Passover: the reason is explained in Pesaḥim, in chapter Kol Sha’ah (Pesaḥim 27b): he derives it from notar.
rashi:b17.2: Impure teruma: is also burned. In Bameh Madlikin (Shabbat 25a) the reason is explained that it is permitted for benefit, as we also say there in chapter Kol Sha’ah (Pesaḥim 23a): “To you it was given, to burn under your cooked food.”
rashi:b17.3: Diverse kinds in a vineyard: “lest the fullness be forfeited [tikdash],” etc. [read as] “lest a fire be kindled [tukad]”; and orla is derived from diverse kinds.
rashi:b17.4: Those whose manner, etc.: refers to orla and diverse kinds in a vineyard: foods are burned and liquids are buried.
tosafot:b17.1: These are the items that are burned: orla and diverse kinds in a vineyard: this requires examination. Granted with regard to diverse kinds in a vineyard, since it is written “lest the fullness be forfeited [tikdash],” [read as] “lest it be kindled [tukad] with fire.” But with regard to orla this requires examination: what is the reason it is burned? And Rashi explained: because it is juxtaposed with diverse kinds in a vineyard.
rashi:b17.5: And one may ignite: to derive benefit from bread and from oil of teruma.
rashi:b17.6: Beyond their time: that is, with the intent to eat them beyond their time or to eat them outside their place.
rashi:b17.7: Shall be burned: as I explained above: it teaches about all the disqualified [items] among consecrated items, etc.
tosafot:b17.2: Items that are burned, their ashes are permitted; items that are buried, their ashes are forbidden [a principle stated in the Gemara on 34a]: this requires examination: what is the reason? And my teacher, the Ramar, says: as for items that are burned, since the verse commanded to burn them, once one has done so it is as though its mitzva has been performed, and there is nothing whose mitzva has been performed that is subject to misuse; here too, since its mitzva has been performed, its prohibition is gone. And that which is said, that an ashera is forbidden forever even though the verse requires it to be burned (Deuteronomy 12), is because it is written: “And there shall cleave nothing of the devoted thing to your hand” (Deuteronomy 13). But items that are buried, which the verse did not require to be burned, their prohibition continues forever.
